questions.question: What is Amazon EBS and why is it needed for EC2?
questions.answer: Amazon EBS (Elastic Block Storage) is a network-attached, persistent block storage service for EC2 instances. EC2 instances are virtual servers that need storage for the operating system, applications, and data — similar to how a laptop needs a hard disk. Without EBS, there is nowhere to store files, configurations, or the OS itself.

questions.question: How is EBS different from Instance Store?
questions.answer: EBS is network-attached storage that persists independently of the EC2 instance lifecycle — data survives stops, reboots, and terminations. Instance Store is a physical disk directly on the host machine running your EC2 instance — it offers higher raw I/O performance but is ephemeral, meaning all data is permanently lost when the instance is stopped or terminated.

questions.question: What are the five EBS volume types and when would you use each?
questions.answer: 1. gp2/gp3 (General Purpose SSD) — most workloads, web servers, dev/test. 2. io1 (Provisioned IOPS SSD) — mission-critical databases needing high IOPS. 3. st1 (Throughput Optimized HDD) — Big Data, data warehouses, high sequential throughput. 4. sc1 (Cold HDD) — infrequently accessed archives, lowest cost. 5. EBS Magnetic — legacy type for infrequently accessed data (being phased out).

questions.question: What is the difference between IOPS and Throughput?
questions.answer: IOPS (Input/Output Operations Per Second) counts the number of read/write operations the disk performs each second — critical for small, random I/O like databases. Throughput measures how much data (MB/s) moves per second — critical for large sequential reads/writes like video streaming or Big Data. Same IOPS with larger file sizes means higher throughput.

questions.question: What is an EBS Snapshot and how do incremental snapshots work?
questions.answer: An EBS Snapshot is a point-in-time backup of an EBS volume stored durably in Amazon S3. The first snapshot is a full copy of the volume. Every subsequent snapshot is incremental — only blocks that changed since the last snapshot are saved. Despite this, restoring from any single snapshot gives you the complete volume state at that point in time.

questions.question: What does it mean to format a disk, and why is it required before using a new EBS volume?
questions.answer: Formatting a disk means preparing it with a filesystem (like XFS or ext4) so the operating system knows how to organize and store files on it. A brand-new EBS volume is raw storage — like a blank notebook with no ruled lines. Without formatting, Linux cannot write files, create folders, or store metadata. You run mkfs.xfs /dev/nvme1n1 to format, then mount it to a directory so the OS can access it.

questions.question: Can you attach an EBS volume from us-east-1a to an EC2 instance in us-east-1b?
questions.answer: No. EBS volumes are scoped to a specific Availability Zone. A volume in us-east-1a can only attach to EC2 instances also in us-east-1a. To use the data in a different AZ, you take a snapshot of the volume and create a new volume from that snapshot in the target AZ.

questions.question: What happens to an EBS volume when you terminate an EC2 instance?
questions.answer: By default, the root EBS volume (boot disk) is deleted when the instance terminates because 'Delete on Termination' is enabled for root volumes. Additional (non-root) EBS volumes are NOT deleted by default — they persist and continue to incur storage charges until you manually delete them. This setting can be changed at launch time.

questions.question: What is the key difference between gp2 and gp3?
questions.answer: gp2 ties IOPS to volume size (3 IOPS per GB, max 16,000 IOPS) — you cannot set IOPS independently. gp3 decouples performance from storage: IOPS (up to 16,000) and throughput (up to 1,000 MB/s) are configurable independently of the disk size. gp3 is approximately 20% cheaper than gp2, and AWS recommends migrating from gp2 to gp3.

questions.question: Which EBS volume types cannot be used as a boot volume?
questions.answer: st1 (Throughput Optimized HDD) and sc1 (Cold HDD) cannot be used as boot volumes. Boot volumes require the fast random-access performance of SSDs. Only gp2, gp3, io1, and io2 can serve as root/boot volumes.

questions.question: Walk me through the steps to expand an EC2 root volume from 8 GB to 20 GB without downtime.
questions.answer: (Situation) The root EBS volume was nearly full at 8 GB. (Task) Expand it to 20 GB with zero instance downtime. (Action) 1. In the EC2 console, modified the volume size from 8 GB to 20 GB. 2. Connected to the instance and ran lsblk to confirm the OS sees 20 GB. 3. Ran sudo growpart /dev/nvme0n1 1 to expand the partition. 4. Ran sudo xfs_growfs -d / to grow the XFS filesystem. 5. Confirmed with df -h that the filesystem now shows 20 GB. (Result) Storage expanded live with no reboot or downtime.

questions.question: Describe how you would attach and configure a new EBS volume for additional storage on a running EC2 instance.
questions.answer: (Situation) The existing root volume was insufficient for growing application data. (Task) Add a second 50 GB EBS volume without disrupting the running application. (Action) 1. Created a new gp3 EBS volume in the same AZ as the instance. 2. Attached it via the EC2 console — it appeared as /dev/nvme1n1. 3. Ran lsblk to confirm attachment. 4. Ran sudo mkfs.xfs /dev/nvme1n1 to format. 5. Created a mount point: sudo mkdir /data. 6. Mounted: sudo mount /dev/nvme1n1 /data. 7. Added entry to /etc/fstab for persistence across reboots. (Result) Application data directory moved to the new 50 GB volume, root disk freed up.

questions.question: A developer accidentally terminated an EC2 instance. How would you recover the data?
questions.answer: (Situation) EC2 instance terminated unexpectedly. (Task) Recover data without losing files. (Action) 1. Checked if the EBS volume survived — by default, non-root volumes persist after termination. 2. Found the unattached EBS volume in the EC2 console under Volumes. 3. Launched a new EC2 instance in the same AZ. 4. Attached the rescued volume to the new instance. 5. Mounted it and confirmed data integrity. (Result) All application data recovered successfully. Lesson: Enable backups via snapshots and review Delete on Termination settings.

questions.question: How would you migrate an EBS volume from one AWS Region to another?
questions.answer: (Situation) Need to replicate a production volume from us-east-1 to ap-south-1 for DR. (Task) Move volume data cross-region. (Action) 1. Took a snapshot of the source EBS volume in us-east-1. 2. Used 'Copy Snapshot' to copy it to ap-south-1. 3. In ap-south-1, created a new EBS volume from the copied snapshot. 4. Attached to target EC2 instance in ap-south-1. (Result) Data successfully replicated cross-region. Snapshots are the only supported path for cross-AZ and cross-Region EBS migration.

questions.question: When would you choose Instance Store over EBS?
questions.answer: (Situation) Building a high-performance caching layer for a web application. (Task) Maximize disk I/O for temporary data. (Action) Selected an instance type with NVMe Instance Store. Used Instance Store for Redis/Memcached temporary data since it offered highest raw I/O performance with no network overhead. All persistent data remained on EBS. (Result) Cache hit latency reduced significantly. Instance Store is ideal for: temporary buffers, caches, scratch space, or replicated data where loss is acceptable.

questions.question: How do you ensure EBS volumes are automatically backed up?
questions.answer: (Situation) Production database volumes had no backup strategy. (Task) Implement automated, consistent backups. (Action) 1. Enabled Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM) to create snapshot policies. 2. Configured daily snapshots with 7-day retention. 3. Tagged volumes so DLM policies applied automatically to new volumes. 4. Verified snapshots in the Snapshots section of the EC2 console. (Result) Automated daily backups in place, RPO reduced to 24 hours.

questions.question: What is horizontal scaling (scale-out) in the context of EBS storage?
questions.answer: (Situation) A data processing application needed more storage than a single EBS volume could provide efficiently. (Task) Add capacity without replacing the existing volume. (Action) Created additional EBS volumes in the same AZ and attached them to the EC2 instance. Used LVM (Logical Volume Manager) to combine volumes into a single logical storage pool. (Result) Storage capacity expanded without downtime or data loss.

questions.question: You find several unattached EBS volumes in your AWS account at month end. What do you do?
questions.answer: (Situation) Cost review shows orphaned EBS volumes incurring charges after EC2 instances were terminated. (Task) Identify and clean up unnecessary storage costs. (Action) 1. Audited all volumes in EC2 console, filtered by 'Available' state (unattached). 2. Cross-referenced with team to confirm volumes are no longer needed. 3. Took final snapshots as insurance before deletion. 4. Deleted the orphaned volumes. 5. Set up AWS Cost Explorer alerts for future orphaned volumes. (Result) Monthly EBS costs reduced significantly.

questions.question: Walk me through taking a manual EBS snapshot and creating a new volume from it.
questions.answer: (Situation) Needed a copy of production volume for testing. (Task) Clone the volume safely via snapshot. (Action) 1. In EC2 console → Volumes, right-clicked the target volume → Create Snapshot. 2. Named and described the snapshot. 3. Waited for snapshot completion (visible in Snapshots section). 4. Right-clicked the snapshot → Create Volume. 5. Selected target AZ, volume type, and size. 6. Attached new volume to a test EC2 instance. (Result) Exact production copy available for testing without touching production data.

questions.question: A company requires 100,000 IOPS for a database cluster. Which storage strategy would you recommend?
questions.answer: (Situation) High-frequency transactional database requiring extreme IOPS. (Task) Architect storage to meet 100,000 IOPS requirement. (Action) Used multiple io1 volumes (each up to 64,000 IOPS) and striped them using RAID 0 or LVM across the volumes. Alternatively, considered local NVMe Instance Store on storage-optimized instances (i3/i3en) which can exceed 100,000 IOPS. Ensured EBS snapshots for any persistent io1 volumes. (Result) IOPS requirement met. Evaluated trade-off: Instance Store = higher performance but ephemeral; io1 = persistent but network-bound.

questions.question: Explain the EBS volume type selection decision framework for an AWS Certified Solutions Architect exam.
questions.answer: Ask three questions: 1. Is performance the priority? → If highest IOPS (>16,000): io1. If balanced price/performance: gp3 (preferred over gp2). 2. Is it throughput/sequential access? → Big Data/warehousing: st1. Cold/archival data: sc1. 3. Is this a boot volume? → Only SSDs (gp2, gp3, io1, io2) can boot. Eliminate st1 and sc1 for any boot scenario. Key numbers: gp2 max = 16,000 IOPS. io1 max = 64,000 IOPS. st1 max = 500 MB/s. sc1 max = 250 MB/s.

questions.question: How does EBS fit into the broader AWS storage ecosystem alongside EFS and S3?
questions.answer: EBS: Block storage — attached to a single EC2 instance in one AZ. Like a private hard disk. Best for databases, OS, applications. EFS: Shared file storage — mounted by multiple EC2 instances simultaneously across AZs. Like a network file share. Best for shared web assets, content management. S3: Object storage — accessed via HTTP/API, infinitely scalable, globally accessible. Like cloud file storage (Dropbox). Best for backups, static websites, data lakes. The three services complement each other: EBS for compute-attached storage, EFS for shared access, S3 for durable object storage.

questions.question: What are the cost implications of different EBS volume types and how would you optimize EBS spend?
questions.answer: Cost hierarchy (lowest to highest per GB): sc1 ($0.025) < st1 ($0.045) < gp2/gp3 ($0.08-0.10) < io1 ($0.125 + $0.065/provisioned IOPS). Optimization strategies: 1. Migrate gp2 → gp3 (20% cheaper, better performance). 2. Delete unattached/orphaned volumes. 3. Use sc1 for cold archival instead of gp2. 4. Right-size volumes — don't provision 100 GB if you use 20 GB. 5. Manage snapshots — delete old ones. 6. Use AWS Compute Optimizer recommendations for volume type changes.

questions.question: What is the relationship between EBS snapshots and AMIs?
questions.answer: An AMI (Amazon Machine Image) is built from EBS snapshots. When you create an AMI from a running EC2 instance, AWS takes snapshots of all attached EBS volumes. Those snapshots power the AMI. When you launch a new instance from the AMI, AWS creates new EBS volumes from those snapshots. This relationship means: AMIs carry storage cost (via underlying snapshots), copying AMIs across Regions copies the snapshots, and deregistering an AMI does NOT automatically delete its snapshots — you must delete them separately.

questions.question: How would you design a highly available storage architecture for a production database on EC2?
questions.answer: Design: 1. Use io1/io2 EBS volumes for the database data directory (high IOPS, consistent performance). 2. Enable Multi-AZ via EBS snapshot replication or use Amazon RDS (manages this automatically). 3. Automate snapshots with AWS DLM (Data Lifecycle Manager) — daily snapshots, 30-day retention. 4. Store snapshots in a separate Region for disaster recovery. 5. Use gp3 for logs and temp directories. 6. Configure CloudWatch alarms on VolumeReadOps, VolumeWriteOps, and BurstBalance metrics. 7. Test restore procedure quarterly. This gives RPO of hours (snapshots) or near-zero (with synchronous replication).
